name: Aaron Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does an ordinary working day involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Aaron, 43, and have a music bachelor’s. I play guitar for a regional theatre, record short guitar parts for local adverts, and teach four pupils on Tuesdays. I have worked long enough to know where a band needs steady rhythm; I am a good working player, not the best soloist in town. I like finding a sound that helps an actor without stealing the scene, and I dislike revising a recording after the client has called it final.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does the family rely on from those jobs?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner runs the accounts at a family-owned garage, and our two children are in school. We have a mortgage, my pay is high for a musician, and we have about seven months of expenses saved. There are plenty of nearby teaching and stage jobs, though a listing is not an offer. I use AI now and then to sort bookings, then check each date with the theatre manager.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the theatre that a quicker booking sheet helps if my show fee still arrives on time. A guitarist has to watch the actor, not just a clock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The mortgage is comfortable with our seven-month reserve and my partner’s steady accounts job. I still want the advert client to pay for revisions, because one unpaid morning adds up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep the theatre dates, four pupils and advert sessions this winter. I would ask for the next paid show schedule in writing and put part of each cleared advert fee into our mortgage reserve after food and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about this mild version. The theatre may change its forms, but one delayed fee will not change our children’s meals.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which revision did you stop doing for free?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A client asked for a softer guitar ending after approving the first one. I gave them a price before opening the recording again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use a tool for a pupil’s lesson?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I sometimes use AI to sort my dates, not to judge a child’s playing. I would listen to the pupil with my own ears before changing an exercise.

say: I would accept a faster **booking sheet** if paid show fees stay clear.
I would tell the theatre that **live guitar** follows an actor’s timing.
think: Our **seven-month reserve** and two incomes cover one delayed fee.
Unpaid **advert revisions** still use a musician’s working morning.
do: Keep **theatre, pupils and adverts** this winter.
Confirm **paid show dates** and save part of cleared advert fees after bills.
feel: I feel **calm** because the mortgage and meals remain covered.
S0.quote: A guitarist has to watch the actor, not just a clock.
fieldNote: His **strong reserve** and partner’s steady work protect the household from a routine delay.
He uses **AI occasionally** for dates and checks lessons with his own ears.

steps.text: Keep paid theatre dates, four pupils and advert sessions this winter
Save part of each cleared advert fee after mortgage, food and bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell clients that cheap generated guitar parts will appear before a robot walks into the theatre pit. I would ask the studio to put revision fees and permission to reuse a part on the invoice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Advert guitar parts supply nearly a third of my music pay. If buyers stop calling, we have months to adjust, but a large piece of my income would go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I’d learn a new AI chord-checker on guitar files I own, compare every suggested chord by playing it, and keep pupil recordings out of the tool. In the first year, if advert orders fall, I’d ask the studio for written reuse fees and stop hiring the extra recording booth on days without a paid session.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about my own studio income, even with seven months saved. Seven months in the bank cannot play a paid advert part for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the checker need to prove?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would have to catch a wrong chord in one of my own parts without inventing another. I would play the change against the actual theatre score before using it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a new tool replace your lessons?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can use a checker for my own score work and still teach the pupil myself. I would not upload a child’s guitar take to test a feature.

I would explain that **generated guitar parts** compete with paid advert work first.
think: Advert parts bring nearly **one third** of my music pay.
The **reserve** buys time, but does not replace that fee.
do: Learn new **AI chord checks** on owned files, playing each suggestion against the theatre score and excluding pupil recordings.
Ask for **reuse fees** if adverts fall; cancel booth hire on days without a paid session.
feel: I feel **anxious** about losing a large part of my own recording pay.
S1.quote: Seven months in the bank cannot play a paid advert part for me.
fieldNote: His **new AI learning** checks chords on owned tracks with playing and score verification.
A likely **advert decline** drives written reuse terms and cuts empty booth hire.

steps.text: Learn AI chord checker on owned guitar files; play each suggestion against theatre score, excluding pupils

Stop extra booth hire on unpaid days if advert orders fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the theatre that thinking AGI by 2028 could make advert guitar parts and booking plans cheaply, while capable robot players follow around 2031. I would ask for the live season in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect advert parts to lose buyers in 2028, and the theatre might shorten a season before any robot plays. Seven months saved gives us time, but a lost third of my pay would still reach the mortgage plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Before 2028 I’d get the theatre’s written paid dates and keep four pupils. In the first year after AGI arrives, if advert orders stop, I’d end the extra booth rental at renewal and audition for an advertised paid theatre guitar seat only if the venue accepts my degree and experience and its written net fee covers travel and confirmed childcare; I’d keep current theatre dates and pupils until a signed offer arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about losing a third of music income, though I can still search nearby. I will not call an audition a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why insist on an offer in writing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have watched a venue advertise a seat and then cancel the show. I would not give up four pupils for an email inviting me to audition.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who covers the children during an audition?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner can collect them on some garage days, but not all. I would confirm a paid sitter before promising a venue a late rehearsal.

say: I would separate **2028 thinking AGI** from robot guitarists around 2031.
I would ask for **written theatre dates** before counting live fees.
think: I expect **advert parts** to lose buyers, perhaps a third of my pay.
Our **seven-month savings** cannot replace that income indefinitely.
do: Keep **theatre and pupils** until signed seat offer; confirm paid dates before 2028.
End **booth rental** at renewal if 2028 adverts stop.
Seek **advertised guitar seat** if adverts stop, credentials accepted and written net fee covers travel and confirmed childcare.
feel: I feel **anxious** about a likely loss of my recording income.
S2.quote: I would not give up four pupils for an email inviting me to audition.
fieldNote: His **advert loss** could precede robot guitarists by about three years.
He keeps **current pay** until a real offer with accepted credentials, written net fee and childcare.

steps.text: Keep paid theatre dates and four pupils until signed guitar-seat offer
End extra booth rental at renewal if 2028 adverts stop
Seek advertised guitar seat if 2028 adverts stop, credentials accepted, written net fee covers travel/confirmed childcare

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my family that five years could let me learn to repair instruments as paid work, not only play them. Thinking AGI reaches recorded parts around 2031, while capable guitar-playing robots come around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A repair shop might value a careful player, but I have not trained to repair other people’s instruments safely. I would not leave a well-paid stage for a course brochure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This spring I’d ask a local guitar-repair shop which posted technician jobs accept its short paid apprenticeship, meaning supervised repair work, and whether it pays training hours. I’d start only if the shop has a real paid place, training costs do not use the mortgage reserve, classes miss no paid theatre dates and pickup is covered; in the first year after 2031, if advert fees end, I’d apply for an open repair role only after completing accepted training, and accept only with a written net offer covering travel and childcare, while keeping shows until an offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious because the advert work can vanish within five years, but I have time to learn a trade properly. A guitar-repair course without a paid shop place is an expense, not a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would an apprentice actually do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would learn to change strings, check a loose cable socket and set up an instrument under supervision. I would not take a customer’s guitar home to practise on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the shop cannot pay training hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep theatre work and four pupils and look for another posted place. I would not spend our mortgage reserve on an unpaid promise.

say: I would explain that **2031 thinking AGI** precedes robot guitarists around 2034.
I would look for a **paid repair apprenticeship** with a real shop.
think: I cannot claim **repair skill** before supervised training.
A course without **paid shop hours** could cost more than it returns.
do: Check **posted repair roles** and paid apprenticeship terms this spring.
Start **repair training** only with real paid place, covered costs, no lost theatre dates and pickup.
Seek **open repair role** after 2031 only if adverts end, training accepted and written net offer covers travel/childcare; keep shows until offer.
feel: I feel **anxious** about advert loss while testing a paid route.
S3.quote: A guitar-repair course without a paid shop place is an expense, not a plan.
fieldNote: His **repair path** is a new trade, not a claim that a music degree alone qualifies him.
Training requires **paid supervised hours**, no mortgage-reserve cost, preserved shows and pickup.

steps.text: Start paid repair apprenticeship if posted role accepts training, costs covered, shows retained and pickup arranged
Seek repair vacancy after 2031 advert loss if accepted training completed; written net offer covers travel/childcare
Keep paid theatre shows and four pupils until signed repair-job offer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the children that a decade lets us learn both an instrument and how it is kept working. Thinking AGI comes around 2036, with capable robot players around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 I might still play shows, and my partner’s work and our savings make next year manageable. Recorded parts could be worth less by then, so I would want a repair qualification that a real shop accepts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I’d keep the theatre and four pupils and save part of each cleared advert fee after mortgage and food. Over the decade I’d take paid repair training only if a posted shop role accepts it, the shop pays training hours and costs, sessions miss no paid shows and pickup is covered; in the first year after 2036, if advert income ends, I’d seek an open repair job only after finishing that training, and accept only with a written net offer covering travel and childcare, while keeping theatre dates until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the far future of recordings, not afraid of next month’s mortgage. A decade to prepare helps only if a repair shop actually pays an apprentice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy repair equipment now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would use the shop’s supervised bench before buying tools. A cleared advert fee belongs in savings until training is a paid place, not a guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stop playing at 56?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would play as long as a show pays and my hands hold up. The job I take later would need to be real before I leave a current booking.

I would teach the children that **instrument repair** can be paid work.
think: At **53**, live shows may still pay while recordings become less valuable.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because advert fees could go before I find another paid theatre seat. Written live dates, a real venue offer that covers travel and childcare, and a repair shop with a paid place would help. I would not borrow against the mortgage for training.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who pays a musician for a revision after the client approves the first recording. One requested guitar-recording revision can take a full morning away from teaching.

headlineQuote: One requested guitar-recording revision can take a full morning away from teaching.
portrait: Aaron is a **43-year-old guitarist** with a music bachelor’s, theatre work, advert recordings and four pupils.
His **higher pay**, partner’s garage wage, mortgage and seven-month reserve support two school-age children.
He uses **AI occasionally** for dates and newly learns chord checking only on owned guitar files.
Fast AGI threatens **advert parts** before robots play; he considers a real guitar seat and paid supervised repair training.
biggestWorry: He fears **AGI by 2028** could remove advert pay before a viable theatre offer arrives.
whatWouldHelp: Written **theatre dates** and a real guitar-seat offer covering travel and childcare would help.
A **paid repair place** with accepted training could open another route without borrowing.
